title: Human Capability Is Context-Dependent
concise_statement: Performance depends not only on physical or technical ability, but on emotional context, incentives, and perceived stakes.
detailed_explanation: Humans do not operate like machines with fixed output levels. Motivation, fear, urgency, social pressure, and reward perception alter what people are capable of achieving in any given moment.
implications: Observed performance limits are situational.
Stress and incentives can unlock hidden capacity.
Real-world outcomes cannot be fully predicted from laboratory conditions.
Human systems require psychological analysis alongside technical analysis.

title: Economies and Markets Are Emotional Systems
concise_statement: Financial systems are driven as much by emotions and narratives as by measurable fundamentals.
detailed_explanation: Market valuations reflect collective hopes, fears, beliefs, and stories about the future. Numerical fundamentals matter, but investor psychology often dominates short- and medium-term outcomes.
implications: Markets cannot be understood through spreadsheets alone.
Investor sentiment materially affects valuations.
Narratives can overpower fundamentals temporarily or for long periods.
Forecasting requires psychological interpretation.

title: Faith and Belief Are Economic Variables
concise_statement: Confidence and belief can determine economic outcomes even when objective fundamentals remain unchanged.
detailed_explanation: Financial systems often depend on collective trust. A sudden loss or gain of belief can radically alter outcomes independent of measurable fundamentals, because participation itself depends on confidence.
implications: Liquidity and funding depend partly on psychology.
Confidence crises can emerge rapidly.
Trust is an invisible but critical economic input.
Sentiment shifts can overwhelm fundamentals.

title: Economic Value Is Subjective
concise_statement: Value exists because people desire something, regardless of whether the desire appears rational.
detailed_explanation: Markets reflect subjective human preferences rather than objective utility alone. Emotional attachment, social identity, speculation, and cultural narratives can all generate economic value.
implications: Markets are inherently psychological.
Perceived irrationality can still produce real prices.
Understanding demand requires understanding human behavior.
Valuation depends partly on collective belief systems.

title: Overconfidence in Models Creates Fragility
concise_statement: Rigid reliance on quantitative models increases vulnerability to unpredictable human behavior.
detailed_explanation: Models simplify reality and often exclude emotional, irrational, or social variables. Excessive trust in models creates blind spots that become dangerous during unusual or emotionally charged conditions.
implications: Risk management should include uncertainty buffers.
Models should be treated as approximations, not truth.
Qualitative judgment remains essential.
Unexpected outcomes are structurally unavoidable.

title: Reality Often Diverges From Rational Expectations
concise_statement: Human systems frequently behave irrationally while still producing persistent recurring patterns.
detailed_explanation: People act emotionally, socially, and impulsively in ways that violate rational models. Yet these irrational behaviors repeat consistently enough to become enduring system characteristics.
implications: Irrationality is a normal market feature.
Pure logic is insufficient for forecasting.
Emotional dynamics create recurring cycles.
Unexpected behavior should be expected.

title: Different Incentives Create Different Rationalities
concise_statement: What appears irrational from one perspective may be perfectly rational given another person's incentives and time horizon.
detailed_explanation: Individuals and institutions operate under different goals, constraints, incentives, and survival pressures. Actions that seem foolish externally may align logically with internal incentives.
implications: Understanding incentives improves prediction.
Behavior must be interpreted contextually.
Conflicts often arise from mismatched time horizons.
There is rarely a universally rational decision.

title: Financial Bubbles Are Incentive-Driven
concise_statement: People sustain bubbles because participating is highly rewarding while the boom lasts.
detailed_explanation: Economic bubbles persist because participants profit socially, psychologically, and financially from continuing the cycle. Incentives distort judgment and encourage self-delusion.
implications: Booms persist longer than logic suggests.
Participants may believe narratives they financially benefit from.
Incentives can overpower skepticism.
Bubble dynamics are socially reinforced.

title: Stories Overpower Statistics During Emotional Periods
concise_statement: Emotionally vivid narratives dominate abstract statistical reasoning.
detailed_explanation: Humans are more persuaded by relatable stories and visible examples than by statistical probabilities. Emotional salience overwhelms analytical abstraction during decision-making.
implications: Narratives can fuel bubbles and panics.
Statistical warnings may be ignored during booms.
Personal anecdotes influence decisions disproportionately.
Communication framing shapes collective behavior.

title: Greed and Fear Move in Cycles
concise_statement: Human psychology oscillates predictably between excessive optimism and excessive pessimism.
detailed_explanation: Periods of success encourage complacency and overconfidence, while periods of crisis generate fear and despair. Each emotional extreme plants the conditions for its opposite.
implications: Market cycles are psychologically driven.
Emotional extremes create future reversals.
Crowd behavior amplifies cyclical instability.
Contrarian thinking becomes valuable at extremes.
